analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, counties, and tribes build and run their own broadband networks despite state bans.
analysis.headline: The Community Broadband Act, which would have struck down state laws blocking city-owned broadband, died in the Senate Commerce Committee with 6 cosponsors and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Many states have laws that stop cities, counties, and tribes from offering their own internet service, even where private companies provide poor or expensive service. This bill would have invalidated those bans nationwide. It paired that with safeguards: public networks would have to play by the same rules as private competitors, public-private partnerships would be encouraged, and there would be no federal bailouts for failed city projects.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents in places where one or two companies control internet access and state law blocks a public alternative — the bill would let local governments or tribes step in and compete, typically lowering prices and improving service. Local governments, public utilities, and tribes that want to build networks would gain the legal right to do so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents stuck with monopoly broadband providers

how_it_helps.text: It overrides any state, local, or tribal law that prohibits or substantially blocks a public provider — a state, a city, or a tribe — from offering broadband or telecom services, restoring the option of a publicly owned network wherever private providers dominate.

It requires public networks to apply the same rules — rights-of-way, permitting, bonding, reporting — to themselves as to private competitors, so the new competition cannot gain through regulatory favoritism, with a narrow exception during declared emergencies.
It protects taxpayers by barring federal funds from reviving a municipal broadband project that went bankrupt or was terminated, except in federally declared disaster areas.
It states Congress's view that public providers should consider public-private partnerships before building, signaling a preference for sharing risk and work with private firms.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent broadband and cable companies, which would face new public competition in markets where state bans currently protect them. Local taxpayers would bear the risk if a publicly built network fails financially, though the bill forbids federal rescue of failed projects.

drawbacks.text: Municipal broadband projects can and do fail financially, and local taxpayers — not the companies or the federal government — would eat those losses; the bill prohibits federal bailouts of failed projects, leaving that risk entirely with local residents.

Critics of municipal broadband argue that city networks, which can borrow at lower rates and avoid some private costs, can undercut private providers unfairly; the bill's anti-favoritism rules address regulation and permitting but do not equalize financing or tax treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — a legal path to publicly owned internet in states that currently ban it — is broad, and the design is cautious rather than aggressive: it imposes nondiscrimination rules on public networks, encourages public-private partnerships, and cuts off federal rescues of failed projects. The main honest cost is local financial risk on projects that don't pan out, which the bill concentrates on local taxpayers. On balance the safeguards address the standard objections without removing the core right to compete.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from May 2020 until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Booker introduced the bill on May 7, 2020, joined by six original cosponsors — four Democrats and two Independents.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent broadband and cable companies are better off, because the state laws that shield them from public competition remain in force in the states that have them. Cities, tribes, and residents in those states gained nothing.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 7, 2020 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Major broadband and cable companies
against.what_they_did: Have long supported the state laws banning or restricting municipal broadband that this bill would have overridden.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested; all seven sponsors were Democrats or Independents, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Broadband and cable incumbents (Comcast, AT&T, Charter and similar providers)
industries.note: Roughly twenty states restrict or ban city-owned broadband networks, rules the industry has supported because they keep public competitors out of monopoly markets. This bill would have voided those restrictions nationwide, exposing incumbents to competition precisely where they are most protected today.

industries.industry: Municipal utilities, cities, and tribal broadband providers
industries.note: The bill would give these public providers the legal right to offer internet service anywhere, subject to the same permitting and rights-of-way rules as private competitors. Their gain comes by serving residents that private networks under-serve or overcharge.
